charts.title: What each coder needs per character on three texts.
charts.takeaway: On the declaration the two language models need 0.27 and 0.57 bits per character against 2.83 for xz; on unseen text they need 1.59 and 1.66, and trained PPM (2.89) does worse than untrained PPM (2.70).
charts.units: bits per character (the average number of bits a coder needs to store one character; lower is better compression). A language model is used as a coder by turning its next-token probabilities into bits
charts.n: English declaration of human rights, 10,637 characters; Unseen text written after the models were released, 30,000 characters; Alice in Wonderland, 30,000 characters; each coder run once on each text
charts.no_interval: Each value is one coder run once on one text. The result files hold no interval.
charts.baseline: xz and untrained PPM have seen no text before the one they code
charts.threshold: Forecasts set in advance had to land within 25 percent: 5 of 8 held, and all 3 that failed are language-model rows that came in far lower than forecast. The unseen text was added after the forecasts.

charts.takeaway: SmolLM2 goes from 0.27 to 1.59 bits per character, 5.9 times as many, while untrained PPM moves only from 2.57 to 2.70: the unseen text is about as hard in itself.

charts.title: What it costs to send a right answer and a wrong one, given the question.
charts.takeaway: A right capital city costs about 1 bit and a wrong one 18.3 to 19.5; a right three-digit sum still costs 8.5 to 9.1 bits, so the models recall capitals and do not reliably add.
charts.units: mean code length in bits of the answer given its prompt (the bits the model needs to store the answer; fewer bits means the model expected it more)
charts.n: Capital cities: 20 prompts; One-digit sums: 30 prompts; Three-digit sums: 30 prompts; one right and one wrong answer per prompt
charts.no_interval: Each value is a mean over the prompts of one task. The result file holds every prompt's bits and no interval.
charts.baseline: A model that knows the answer needs close to 0 bits for it
charts.threshold: Set in advance for Qwen3: a right three-digit sum costs at least 10 bits. Failed, 9.11

axis.label: bits to send the answer (fewer means more expected)

charts.title: Does PPM's training gain come from the order of the training text?
charts.takeaway: Yes: training takes PPM from 2.57 to 1.99 bits per character on the declaration; training on the same characters shuffled gives 3.59, worse than no training, and on shuffled words 2.10.
charts.units: bits per character (the average number of bits a coder needs to store one character; lower is better compression). PPM (prediction by partial matching) is a classical coder that predicts each character from the few before it
charts.n: 5,000,000 training characters; scored on the 10,637 characters of the declaration; one run per training set
charts.no_interval: Each value is one training run scored once. The result file holds no interval.
charts.threshold: Character shuffling must remove at least 0.8 of the training gain, set in advance: held, it removed 2.74 times the gain. Word shuffling removed 0.20 of it.

axis.label: bits per character on the declaration (lower is better)

charts.title: Are the model rows real codes that decode back to the text?
charts.takeaway: Yes: a 120-token passage was coded into 306 bits by SmolLM2 and 444 bits by Qwen3, and the decoder returned the same tokens and the same text both times.
charts.units: each row compares the decoder's output with the input of an arithmetic coder (a coder that turns a model's predicted probabilities into a string of bits)
charts.n: one passage of 120 tokens per model (614 and 618 characters)
charts.no_interval: Each row is an exact comparison of one decoded passage with its input.
charts.threshold: An inexact round trip would have voided the model rows, set in advance. It did not happen.
charts.baseline: The long-document values in the other charts are ideal code lengths summed from the model's probabilities, not coded bit strings
